plan.why: An evergreen cost and access worry refreshed by new JAMA Health Forum data. A save-and-share checklist fits the carousel format, and it pushes viewers away from unsafe sources, in line with the brand guardrails. | fact-check: Verified (UGA Today, JAMA Health Forum 2026): 8,914 continuously insured US adults who started GLP-1s for weight loss over a 1.5-year study period. The study is observational (claims-based). Out-of-pocket bands were $0–21, $22–43, $44–75, $76–168 and >$168. Adjusted non-adherence was 74.7–76.6% across the 3 cheapest bands, 79.7% at $76–168 and 85.2% above $168. Problems: (1) 'Above 80% once costs passed $75' is press-release framing. The $76–168 band was 79.7% adjusted, so use the paper's adjusted band figures, not 'rose above 80%'. (2) 'About 3 in 4 stopped within a year' may confuse non-adherence (probably a proportion-of-days-covered threshold, i.e. missing doses) with stopping. Use the paper's exact definition and don't say 'stopped' unless the paper does. (3) Confirm which GLP-1s were included (one write-up says semaglutide) and the insurance type (commercial?). (4) Medicare: anti-obesity GLP-1 coverage and the $50 cap programme are changing in 2026. Verify the exact eligibility and dates against CMS/Medicare.gov, hedge with 'as of Sept 2026', and don't imply all Medicare enrollees qualify. (5) Manufacturer savings and direct-pay programmes are fine if they come from the official manufacturer site, with their limits stated (commercial insurance only; usually not valid with government insurance). Keep the warning against compounded, gray-market and 'research' products, and the 'don't stop or change your dose to save money without talking to your prescriber' line.

package.title: Semaglutide Cost and Adherence: What Changed Above $75 a Month, and Legit Questions to Ask (US)

social.facebook_caption:
New research looked at 8,914 commercially insured US adults with obesity (no type 2 diabetes) who started semaglutide for weight loss in 2021–22, and tracked their pharmacy records for a year.

The pattern: as monthly out-of-pocket costs rose, so did non-adherence (having medicine on hand less than 80% of days) — from 74.7–76.6% at $0–75/month to 79.7% at $76–168/month to 85.2% above $168/month, adjusted for other factors. This is observational, so it shows a link, not proof that cost alone caused it. And even in the cheapest group, about 3 in 4 people weren't consistently stocked up, so cost isn't the whole story. (Low supply isn't the same as quitting, and people started in 2021–22, before newer drugs and today's price programs.)

If cost is a worry, it can help to ask your insurer about your formulary, prior authorization, and appeals before you fill a prescription, and to loop in your doctor or pharmacist rather than stretching, skipping, or stopping on your own.

factcheck.summary: The carousel is accurate and safe, so it passes. I checked the key sources directly. JAMA Health Forum (Shin et al., published Aug 28, 2026) says what the slides say: 8,914 commercially insured adults with obesity and no type 2 diabetes, who started semaglutide between June 2021 and December 2022 and were each followed for 1 year. Non-adherence means medicine on hand for less than 80% of days. The adjusted rates are 74.7% (Q1) to 76.6% (Q3) in the $0–75 bands, 79.7% at $76–168 and 85.2% above $168, with a threshold at about $75. The slides frame it correctly as observational ("linked, not proven cause") and say non-adherence isn't the same as quitting. The CMS GLP-1 Bridge page confirms the Jul 1, 2026–Dec 31, 2027 dates, the strict eligibility criteria and that it applies to weight management only. The FDA page confirms what the slides say about compounded drugs: not approved, not reviewed for safety, effectiveness or quality, and linked to dosing-error reports. It also confirms that some products are falsely labeled 'for research'. The HealthCare.gov appeals page exists and covers internal and external appeals. Safety is handled well: no dosing or switching advice, the 'don't do alone' column on slide 7, a warning against gray-market sellers, and the exact prescriber line on the CTA. The fixes below are wording polish plus one source to drop: the UGA press release gives numbers that don't match the paper.

issues.claim: Higher GLP-1 costs lead to lower adherence (UGA Today)
issues.problem: The press release says 75% 'discontinued' the medicine in the lowest cost tier and gives 'about 83%' non-adherence above $168. The paper measured non-adherence (less than 80% of days covered), not discontinuation, and reports an adjusted 85.2% above $168. The press release also says the study used GLP-1s in general, but the paper is about semaglutide only. Its numbers don't match the primary source.
issues.fix: Remove S2 from the source list and cite only S1 (JAMA Health Forum) for the study figures.

issues.claim: Adjusted 74.7–76.6% at $0–75 a month had medicine on hand for less than 80% of days in year 1... Data from 2021–22
issues.problem: The grammar is awkward. Also, '2021–22' is when people started the medicine, not the whole data period: follow-up ran into 2023.
issues.fix: At $0–75 a month, an adjusted 74.7–76.6% had medicine on hand for less than 80% of days in their first year (from pharmacy claims). That isn't the same as quitting. People started in 2021–22, before newer drugs and today's price programs. Source: JAMA Health Forum 2026.

issues.claim: Products labeled "for research" are illegal, unapproved drugs.
issues.problem: FDA's wording is narrower. It says companies illegally sold unapproved drugs that were falsely labeled 'for research purposes' or 'not for human consumption' to consumers for human use.
issues.fix: Products sold for people but falsely labeled "for research" or "not for human consumption" are illegal, unapproved drugs.
